fanoutqa_039337.t: Joshua Angrist :: Honors and awards :: chunk_0008
fanoutqa_039337.x:
Joshua Angrist :: Honors and awards :: chunk_0008
Angrist is a Research Fellow at the [Institute for the Study of Labor](/wiki/Institute_for_the_Study_of_Labor "Institute for the Study of Labor") (IZA). He is also a fellow of the [Econometric Society](/wiki/Econometric_Society "Econometric Society"). He was elected a Fellow of the [American Academy of Arts and Sciences](/wiki/American_Academy_of_Arts_and_Sciences "American Academy of Arts and Sciences") in 2006.[[67]](#cite_note-AAAS-67) In 2007 Angrist received an honorary doctorate in economics from the [University of St. Gallen](/wiki/University_of_St._Gallen "University of St. Gallen"). He is the recipient of the 2011 [John von Neumann Award](/wiki/John_von_Neumann_Award "John von Neumann Award") given annually by the [Rajk László College for Advanced Studies](/wiki/Rajk_L%C3%A1szl%C3%B3_College_for_Advanced_Studies "Rajk László College for Advanced Studies") in Budapest.

Angrist, along with [Guido Imbens](/wiki/Guido_Imbens "Guido Imbens"), won the 2021 [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics](/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economics "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics").[[68]](#cite_note-68) The two men received one-half of the prize money of 10 million Swedish crowns ($1.14 million U.S.); the rest went to the other winner, [David Card](/wiki/David_Card "David Card").[[69]](#cite_note-69) The [Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences](/wiki/Royal_Swedish_Academy_of_Sciences "Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences") wrote that:

> Data from a natural experiment are difficult to interpret... . For example, extending compulsory education by
> a year for one group of students (but not another) will not affect everyone in that group in the same way. Some students would have kept studying anyway and, for them, the value of education is often not representative of the entire group. fanoutqa_018089.t: Digital camera :: History :: 21st-Century and Commercial Usage :: chunk_0003
fanoutqa_018089.x:
Digital camera :: History :: 21st-Century and Commercial Usage :: chunk_0003
The first prototype camera phones were included in [Isaac (camera phone)](/wiki/Isaac_(camera_phone) "Isaac (camera phone)"), a personal digital assistant for people with intellectual disabilities which was deployed in 1994.[[26]](#cite_note-26) The first commercially available [camera phone](/wiki/Camera_phone "Camera phone") was the [Kyocera](/wiki/Kyocera "Kyocera") Visual Phone VP-210, released in Japan in May 1999.[[27]](#cite_note-computerworld-27) It was called a "mobile videophone" at the time,[[28]](#cite_note-28) and had a 110,000-[pixel](/wiki/Pixel "Pixel") [front-facing camera](/wiki/Front-facing_camera "Front-facing camera").[[27]](#cite_note-computerworld-27) It stored up to 20 JPEG [digital images](/wiki/Digital_image "Digital image"), which could be sent over e-mail, or the phone could send up to two images per second over Japan's [Personal Handy-phone System](/wiki/Personal_Handy-phone_System "Personal Handy-phone System") (PHS) [cellular network](/wiki/Cellular_network "Cellular network").[[27]](#cite_note-computerworld-27)

The [Samsung](/wiki/Samsung "Samsung") SCH-V200, released in [South Korea](/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea") in June 2000, was also one of the first phones with a built-in camera. It had a [TFT](/wiki/Thin-film_transistor "Thin-film transistor") [liquid-crystal display](/wiki/Liquid-crystal_display "Liquid-crystal display") (LCD) and stored up to 20 [digital photos](/wiki/Digital_photography "Digital photography") at 350,000-pixel resolution. However, it could not send the resulting image over the telephone function but required a computer connection to access photos.[[29]](#cite_note-digitaltrends-29) The first mass-market camera phone was the [J-SH04](/wiki/J-SH04 "J-SH04"), a [Sharp](/wiki/Sharp_Corporation "Sharp Corporation") [J-Phone](/wiki/J-Phone "J-Phone") model sold in Japan in November 2000.[[30]](#cite_note-30)[[29]](#cite_note-digitaltrend

fanoutqa_006569.x:
Taj Mahal :: Architecture and design :: Exterior :: part 01 :: chunk_0005
[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Taj_Mahal_in_India_-_Kristian_Bertel.jpg/250px-Taj_Mahal_in_India_-_Kristian_Bertel.jpg)](/wiki/File:Taj_Mahal_in_India_-_Kristian_Bertel.jpg)

The eight sided main structure with large arched doorways and [minarets](/wiki/Minaret "Minaret") on a square plinth

The mausoleum building is the central structure of the entire complex. It is a white marble structure standing on a 6-metre (20 ft) high square [plinth](/wiki/Plinth "Plinth") with sides measuring 95.5 metres (313 ft) in length. The base structure is a large multi-chambered cube with [chamfered](/wiki/Chamfer "Chamfer") corners forming an eight-sided structure that is approximately 57.3 metres (188 ft) long on each of the four long sides.[[25]](#cite_note-ASI-25)

The building has four identical sides with *[iwans](/wiki/Iwan "Iwan")* (arch-shaped doorways), topped by a large dome and [finial](/wiki/Finial "Finial"). Each side of the iwan is framed with a 33-metre (108 ft) high *[pishtaq](/wiki/Pishtaq "Pishtaq")* (vaulted archway) with two similarly shaped arched balconies stacked on either side. This motif of archways is replicated on a smaller scale on the chamfered corner areas, making the design completely symmetrical.[[26]](#cite_note-Brit-26) At the southern side of the platform, facing the garden, there are two flights of stairs on either side which are partly covered and provide the only access from ground level up to the mausoleum building.[[24]](#cite_note-Arch2-24)

fanoutqa_031657.t: One Piece :: Media :: Anime :: 1999 series :: Theatrical films :: chunk_0014
fanoutqa_031657.x:
One Piece :: Media :: Anime :: 1999 series :: Theatrical films :: chunk_0014
Main article: [List of *One Piece* films](/wiki/List_of_One_Piece_films "List of One Piece films")

Fourteen animated theatrical *One Piece* films produced by [Toei Animation](/wiki/Toei_Animation "Toei Animation") have been released. The films are typically released in March to coincide with the spring vacation of Japanese schools.[[57]](#cite_note-10th_Movie-74) They feature self-contained, completely original plots, or alternate retellings of story arcs with animation of a higher quality than that of the regular anime series. The first three films were typically double features paired up with other anime films and were thus usually an hour or less in length. The films themselves offer contradictions in both chronology and design that make them incompatible with a single continuity. Funimation has licensed the eighth, tenth, and twelfth films for release in North America, and these films have received in-house dubs by the company.[[58]](#cite_note-75)[[59]](#cite_note-76)

fanoutqa_009385.t: Mercury (planet) :: Orbit, rotation, and longitude :: part 02 :: chunk_0017
fanoutqa_009385.x:
Mercury (planet) :: Orbit, rotation, and longitude :: part 02 :: chunk_0017
At certain points on Mercury's surface, an observer would be able to see the Sun peek up a little more than two-thirds of the way over the horizon, then reverse and set before rising again, all within the same [Mercurian day](/wiki/Extraterrestrial_skies#Mercury "Extraterrestrial skies").[[a]](#cite_note-angular-117) This is because approximately four Earth days before perihelion, Mercury's angular [orbital velocity](/wiki/Orbital_speed "Orbital speed") equals its angular [rotational velocity](/wiki/Rotational_velocity "Rotational velocity") so that the Sun's [apparent motion](/wiki/Improper_motion "Improper motion") ceases; closer to perihelion, Mercury's angular orbital velocity then exceeds the angular rotational velocity. Thus, to a hypothetical observer on Mercury, the Sun appears to move in a [retrograde](/wiki/Apparent_retrograde_motion "Apparent retrograde motion") direction. Four Earth days after perihelion, the Sun's normal apparent motion resumes.[[28]](#cite_note-strom-28) A similar effect would have occurred if Mercury had been in synchronous rotation: the alternating gain and loss of rotation over a revolution would have caused a libration of 23.65° in longitude.[[117]](#cite_note-118)

For the same reason, there are two points on Mercury's equator, 180 degrees apart in [longitude](/wiki/Longitude "Longitude"), at either of which, around perihelion in alternate Mercurian years (once a Mercurian day), the Sun passes overhead, then reverses its apparent motion and passes overhead again, then reverses a second time and passes overhead a third time, taking a total of about 16 Earth-days for this entire process. In the other alternate Mercurian years, the same thing happens at the other of these two points. fanoutqa_030121.t: London School of Economics :: part 02 :: chunk_0001
fanoutqa_030121.x:
London School of Economics :: part 02 :: chunk_0001
LSE is a member of the [Russell Group](/wiki/Russell_Group "Russell Group"), the [Association of Commonwealth Universities](/wiki/Association_of_Commonwealth_Universities "Association of Commonwealth Universities") and the [European University Association](/wiki/European_University_Association "European University Association"), and is typically considered part of the "[golden triangle](/wiki/Golden_triangle_(universities) "Golden triangle (universities)")" of research universities in the south east of England. The [British Library of Political and Economic Science](/wiki/British_Library_of_Political_and_Economic_Science "British Library of Political and Economic Science"), commonly referred to as "LSE Library", is the main library of the university, and one of the largest libraries in the world devoted to the economic and social sciences.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

Since 1990, the London School of Economics has educated 24 prime ministers or presidents, the second highest number of any university in the United Kingdom, and since the school's founding in 1895, over 40 world leaders, 2 presidents of the [European Commission](/wiki/European_Commission "European Commission"), and 21 Nobel laureates have taught or studied at LSE.[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11)[[12]](#cite_note-12)

"[Heat Waves](/wiki/Heat_Waves "Heat Waves")" by [Glass Animals](/wiki/Glass_Animals "Glass Animals") *(pictured)* was the best-performing single of 2022; in addition, it was #16 on the 2021 Year-End List. It spent five weeks at number one on the weekly chart in 2022, and spent 91 weeks on the chart overall, becoming the longest-charting song in the Hot 100's 64-year history.[[1]](#cite_note-yearend-1)

The [*Billboard* Hot 100](/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") is a chart that ranks the best-performing [singles](/wiki/Single_(music) "Single (music)") of the United States. Its data, published by *[Billboard](/wiki/Billboard_(magazine) "Billboard (magazine)")* magazine and compiled by [Nielsen SoundScan](/wiki/Nielsen_SoundScan "Nielsen SoundScan"), is based collectively on each single's weekly [physical](/wiki/CD_single "CD single") and [digital](/wiki/Digital_distribution "Digital distribution") sales, as well as [airplay](/wiki/Heavy_rotation "Heavy rotation") and [streaming](/wiki/Streaming_media "Streaming media"). At the end of a year, *Billboard* will publish an annual list of the 100 most successful songs throughout that year on the Hot 100 chart based on the information. For 2022, the list was published on December 1, calculated with data from November 20, 2021 to November 12, 2022.[[1]](#cite_note-yearend-1) At the number-one position was [Glass Animals](/wiki/Glass_Animals "Glass Animals")' "[Heat Waves](/wiki/Heat_Waves "Heat Waves")", which spent 5 weeks on top of the *Billboard* Hot 100. It accumulated a total of 91 weeks on the chart, which is the longest-charting song in the 64-year history of the *Billboard* Hot 100.

A **die** (plural: **dice**, sometimes also used as singular)[[1]](#cite_note-1) is a small, throwable object with marked sides that can rest in multiple positions. Dice are used for generating [random values](/wiki/Statistical_randomness "Statistical randomness"), commonly as part of [tabletop games](/wiki/Tabletop_game "Tabletop game"), including [dice games](/wiki/List_of_dice_games "List of dice games"), [board games](/wiki/Board_game "Board game"), [role-playing games](/wiki/Role-playing_game "Role-playing game"), and [games of chance](/wiki/Game_of_chance "Game of chance").

A traditional die is a [cube](/wiki/Cube "Cube") with each of its six faces marked with a different number of dots ([pips](/wiki/Pip_(counting) "Pip (counting)")) from 1 to 6. When thrown or rolled, the die comes to rest showing a random [integer](/wiki/Integer "Integer") from one to six on its upper surface, with each value being equally likely. Dice may also have other [polyhedral](/wiki/Polyhedron "Polyhedron") or irregular shapes, may have faces marked with numerals or symbols instead of pips and may have their numbers carved out from the material of the dice instead of marked on it. **Napoleon Bonaparte**[[b]](#cite_note-2) (born **Napoleone di Buonaparte**;[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDwyer2008axv-3)[[c]](#cite_note-4) 15 August 1769 – 5 May 1821), later known by his [regnal name](/wiki/Regnal_name "Regnal name") **Napoleon I**, was [Emperor of the French](/wiki/Emperor_of_the_French "Emperor of the French") from 18 May 1804 until his [first abdication](/wiki/Napoleon%27s_first_abdication "Napoleon's first abdication") in 1814, with a brief restoration during the [Hundred Days](/wiki/Hundred_Days "Hundred Days") in 1815. He rose to prominence as a [general](/wiki/General_of_division "General of division") during the [French Revolution](/wiki/French_Revolution "French Revolution") and led [a series of military campaigns](/wiki/Military_career_of_Napoleon "Military career of Napoleon") across Europe and the Middle East during the [French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars](/wiki/French_Revolutionary_and_Napoleonic_Wars "French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars"). As a statesman, he implemented numerous legal and administrative reforms in France and Europe.

Born on the island of [Corsica](/wiki/Corsica "Corsica") to a family of Italian origin, Napoleon moved to mainland France in 1779 and was commissioned as an officer in the [French Royal Army](/wiki/French_Royal_Army "French Royal Army") in 1785. He supported the French Revolution in 1789 and promoted its cause in Corsica. He rose rapidly through the ranks after winning the [siege of Toulon](/wiki/Siege_of_Toulon_(1793) "Siege of Toulon (1793)") in 1793 and defeating royalist insurgents in Paris on [13 Vendémiaire](/wiki/13_Vend%C3%A9miaire "13 Vendémiaire") in 1795. Main article: [49ers–Cowboys rivalry](/wiki/49ers%E2%80%93Cowboys_rivalry "49ers–Cowboys rivalry")

The rivalry between the [Dallas Cowboys](/wiki/Dallas_Cowboys "Dallas Cowboys") and the 49ers has lasted since the 1970s. The [NFL Top 10](/wiki/NFL_Top_10 "NFL Top 10") ranked this rivalry to be the tenth best in NFL history. San Francisco has played Dallas in nine postseason games. The Cowboys defeated the 49ers in the 1970 and 1971 NFC Championship Games, and again in the 1972 Divisional Playoff Game. The 1981 NFC Championship Game in San Francisco, which saw the 49ers' [Joe Montana](/wiki/Joe_Montana "Joe Montana") complete a game-winning pass to [Dwight Clark](/wiki/Dwight_Clark "Dwight Clark") in the final minute (now known as **The Catch**), is one of the most famous games in NFL history. The rivalry became even more intense during the 1992–1994 seasons. San Francisco and Dallas faced each other in the NFC Championship Game three separate times. Dallas won the first two match-ups, and San Francisco won the third. In each of these pivotal match-ups, the game's victor went on to win the Super Bowl. Both the Cowboys and the 49ers are third all-time in [Super Bowl](/wiki/Super_Bowl "Super Bowl") victories to the [Pittsburgh Steelers](/wiki/Pittsburgh_Steelers "Pittsburgh Steelers") and [New England Patriots](/wiki/New_England_Patriots "New England Patriots") with five each. The 49ers–Cowboys rivalry is also part of the larger cultural rivalry between California and Texas. In recent years, this once-great rivalry has greatly softened, with the struggles of both the Cowboys and 49ers. However, in its prime especially in the 1990s, this rivalry was a very bitter one as both teams were the class of the NFL during this time. In what was believed to be the greatest upset in the team's rivalry in the modern era, the 49ers upset the Cowboys in the 2021 Wild Card Round.

Languages of Spain

Spain is a multilingual state.[[278]](#cite_note-conversi-295) [Spanish](/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language")—featured in the 1978 [Spanish Constitution](/wiki/Spanish_Constitution "Spanish Constitution") as *castellano* (['Castilian'](/wiki/Names_given_to_the_Spanish_language "Names given to the Spanish language"))—has effectively been the official language of the entire country since 1931.[[279]](#cite_note-296) As allowed in the third article of the Constitution, the other 'Spanish languages' can also become official in their respective [autonomous communities](/wiki/Autonomous_communities "Autonomous communities"). The territoriality created by the form of co-officiality codified in the 1978 Constitution creates an asymmetry, in which Spanish speakers' rights apply to the entire territory whereas vis-à-vis the rest of co-official languages, their speakers' rights only apply in their territories.[[280]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERamallo2018465-297)

Besides Spanish, other territorialised languages include [Aragonese](/wiki/Aragonese_language "Aragonese language"), [Aranese](/wiki/Aranese "Aranese"), [Astur-Leonese](/wiki/Astur-Leonese "Astur-Leonese"), [Basque](/wiki/Basque_language "Basque language"), Ceutan Arabic ([Darija](/wiki/Darija "Darija")), [Catalan](/wiki/Catalan_language "Catalan language")/[Valencian](/wiki/Valencian_language "Valencian language"), [Galician](/wiki/Galician_language "Galician language"), [Portuguese](/wiki/Portuguese_language "Portuguese language") and [Tamazight](/wiki/Tarifit "Tarifit"), to which the [Romani Caló](/wiki/Cal%C3%B3_language "Caló language") and the sign languages may add up.[[281]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERamallo2018462-298)

The [Super Bowl](/wiki/Super_Bowl "Super Bowl") is the annual [American football](/wiki/American_football "American football") game that determines the champion of the [National Football League](/wiki/National_Football_League "National Football League") (NFL). The game culminates a [season](/wiki/National_Football_League_regular_season "National Football League regular season") that begins in the previous calendar year, and is the conclusion of the [NFL playoffs](/wiki/National_Football_League_playoffs "National Football League playoffs"). The winner receives the [Vince Lombardi Trophy](/wiki/Vince_Lombardi_Trophy "Vince Lombardi Trophy"). The contest is held in an American city, chosen three to four years beforehand,[[1]](#cite_note-1) usually at warm-weather sites or [domed stadiums](/wiki/Stadium#Types "Stadium").[[2]](#cite_note-2) Since January 1971, the winner of the [American Football Conference (AFC) Championship Game](/wiki/AFC_Championship_Game "AFC Championship Game") has faced the winner of the [National Football Conference (NFC) Championship Game](/wiki/NFC_Championship_Game "NFC Championship Game") in the culmination of the NFL playoffs.
